sentences.text: The holotype comprises a partial skeleton preserving dorsal and sacral vertebrae, ribs, shoulder elements, a forearm bone, a hand claw, hip and leg bones, ankle bones, and a toe bone.
At roughly 4.5 m long and 222 kg in mass, Musango is among the largest known Late Triassic bipedal dinosaurs from southern Africa.
The specimen was uncovered in March 2018 on the margin of Lake Kariba by a South African and Zimbabwean-led expedition.
It now resides in the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe in Bulawayo under accession code NHMZ 2583.
Paul Barrett and colleagues formally described the find as a new genus and species of sauropodomorph in 2026.
The generic name honors the Musango Archosaur Site near the Musango Safari Camp on Lake Kariba, while the specific epithet refers to nearby Matusadona National Park.
Musango represents the fifth dinosaur genus to be described from Zimbabwe.
Comparisons with better-known relatives suggest Musango was an obligate biped, walking primarily on its hind limbs.
Its estimated length of about 4.5 m and mass of roughly 222 kg indicate a medium-sized Triassic predator or herbivore, depending on diet inferred from related taxa.
Musango is placed within Sauropodomorpha, specifically in the family Unaysauridae.
Phylogenetic analysis recovers it as the sister taxon to Musankwa within the Unaysauridae clade.
The animal lived during the Late Triassic, in the Norian age of the Upper Triassic Pebbly Arkose Formation of Zimbabwe.
